title: Long COVID and Post-infectious Pulmonary Syndromes
summary: Long COVID frequently involves persistent respiratory symptoms with variable objective impairment. Dominant pulmonary phenotypes include dyspnea with normal imaging/PFTs, small-airway disease with air-trapping, post-viral organizing pneumonia, pulmonary vascular disease/PE, and post-COVID interstitial lung disease with fibrotic change. Evidence supports structured evaluation (symptom assessment, pulse oximetry, PFTs with DLCO, 6MWT, chest CT when indicated) and targeted management including pulmonary rehabilitation, cautious steroid trials for organizing pneumonia, and standard evidence-based care for PE. True progressive post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis appears uncommon but clinically significant in selected survivors of severe pneumonia/ARDS.
clinicalQuestion: What are the prevalent pulmonary phenotypes of Long COVID, how common are they, and what evaluation and management pathways are supported by current evidence?

heroStats.label: Global long COVID prevalence after infection
Common respiratory complaints
heroStats.value: Shortness of breath 27%–30% in surveys [3], with cough ≈33% in clinic cohorts [4]

heroStats.label: Most impactful long-term pulmonary morbidity
heroStats.value: Post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis in a subset of severe cases [5], [6], [7]

keyMoments.title: Recognize heterogeneous respiratory phenotypes
keyMoments.body: Long COVID presents with dyspnea, cough, chest pain, and exercise intolerance, often with discordance between symptoms and routine tests. Distinguish small-airway disease, organizing pneumonia, post-PE dyspnea, and fibrotic ILD to guide therapy [1], [2], [8], [9].

keyMoments.title: Structured evaluation is essential
keyMoments.body: Prioritize symptom scores, oximetry at rest and exertion, PFTs with DLCO, 6MWT, and targeted chest CT for persistent symptoms or abnormal tests. Screen for PE when indicated; many abnormalities track with acute severity [10], [8], [9].

keyMoments.title: Rehab improves function across phenotypes
keyMoments.body: Pulmonary rehabilitation and graded, symptom-titrated activity demonstrate clinically meaningful gains in ILD and post-COVID cohorts; integrate breathing retraining and pacing strategies [6].

keyMoments.title: Inflammation vs. fibrosis dictates therapy
keyMoments.body: Suspected organizing pneumonia may respond to corticosteroids, whereas established fibrosis requires supportive care and ILD-directed management; antifibrotics remain investigational in post-COVID fibrosis [6], [9].

keyMoments.title: Do not miss vascular complications
keyMoments.body: Pulmonary embolism and chronic thromboembolic disease contribute to persistent dyspnea; follow standard diagnostic and anticoagulation pathways [11], [9].

sections.title: Pulmonary Manifestations of Long COVID
sections.blurb: Clinically relevant syndromes span airway, interstitial, and vascular compartments with variable imaging and physiological correlates.

steps.title: Dyspnea with normal spirometry and imaging
steps.body: Common and multifactorial: deconditioning, dysfunctional breathing, microvascular dysregulation, or autonomic features. DLCO may be mildly reduced even when spirometry is normal [1], [8].

steps.title: Small-airway disease and air-trapping
steps.body: Patients report exertional dyspnea and cough; expiratory CT may reveal air-trapping despite normal inspiratory CT and spirometry. Severity correlates with acute illness severity [10], [8].

steps.title: Organizing pneumonia (post-viral inflammatory ILD)
steps.body: Persistent ground-glass opacities and perilobular consolidations with subacute dyspnea and cough. Many improve spontaneously; a subset respond to a cautious corticosteroid taper when clinically significant [6], [9].

steps.title: Post-COVID interstitial lung disease with fibrotic change
steps.body: Fibrotic bands, traction, and architectural distortion after severe pneumonia/ARDS. True progressive fibrosis is less common but accounts for significant morbidity; risk scales with acute disease severity [5], [6], [7].

steps.title: Pulmonary vascular disease
steps.body: Acute/subacute pulmonary embolism and sequelae (including chronic thromboembolic disease) present with chest pain, dyspnea, and exercise limitation; maintain a low threshold for imaging in high-risk patients [11], [9].

steps.title: Delayed inflammatory pulmonary syndrome
steps.body: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory condition in the subacute phase (around week 4) with hypoxemia and radiographic progression, requiring prompt recognition and immunomodulatory care [12].

sections.title: Evaluation Algorithm
sections.blurb: Begin broadly, then tailor testing to phenotype and severity.

cards.title: Initial Assessment
items: Symptom inventory: dyspnea, cough, chest pain, exercise intolerance, orthopnea [1], [2]
Vitals and pulse oximetry at rest and with exertion (1-min sit-to-stand or 6MWT) [8]
Baseline labs as indicated (CBC, BMP); consider D-dimer if PE risk features present [9]

cards.title: Physiology
items: Full PFTs with DLCO; DLCO reduction is common and prognostically informative [8], [9]
6MWT with desaturation monitoring; consider CPET for unexplained dyspnea after basic workup [1], [8]

cards.title: Imaging Strategy
items: Chest radiograph if symptoms persist >4–6 weeks post-acute illness [8]
Low-dose inspiratory chest CT for abnormal exam, persistent hypoxemia, or impaired PFTs; add expiratory CT if small-airway disease suspected [10], [9]
CT pulmonary angiography when clinical probability of PE is intermediate/high [11], [9]

cards.title: Red Flags
items: Rest/exertional hypoxemia, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, syncope, rapidly progressive dyspnea [11], [12], [9]

cards.title: Phenotype-Directed Treatment
items: Organizing pneumonia: consider a monitored prednisone taper when clinically significant; reassess with symptoms and PFTs [6], [9]
Suspected fibrosis: supportive care, optimize comorbidities; antifibrotics remain investigational post-COVID [6], [7]
Small-airway disease: trial inhaled bronchodilator ± inhaled corticosteroid case-by-case; incorporate breathing retraining [1], [8]
Pulmonary embolism: standard anticoagulation per guidelines; evaluate for chronic thromboembolic disease if persistent dyspnea [11], [9]

cards.title: Follow-up and Recovery
items: Repeat PFTs and functional testing at 8–12 weeks and every 3–6 months if impaired [8]
Re-image only if symptoms or physiology worsen or fail to improve [9]
Enroll in pulmonary rehabilitation to improve dyspnea, endurance, and quality of life [6]
